parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Score with visible assumptions
parts.body:
Portfolio scoring is a conversation aid, not an oracle. Start with strategic fit, a value range, feasibility, data readiness, adoption effort, risk and time to evidence. Define each scale before scoring. A five on value should mean something observable, such as a credible benefit above an agreed threshold, while a one means little expected change. Put raw measures alongside ordinal scores so executives can inspect annual case volume, minutes per case, customer impact, cash cost, and confidence in each estimate.

Agree on weights before presenting favored proposals. Keep risk visible as a separate dimension or an eligibility gate when an obligation cannot be waived. A weighted total must never imply that a strong revenue estimate compensates for an unlawful data use. NIST's AI RMF asks organizations to map context and impacts, measure performance, and manage risk responses. It does not prescribe a universal scoring formula; the company must decide its own constraints and risk appetite.

Score a range rather than false precision where evidence is thin. Mark assumptions as observed, estimated, or unknown. An uncertain candidate may deserve a small discovery budget even if its initial score is modest. Record who provided each estimate and when it will be revisited. The portfolio review should know whether it is allocating scale capital or paying to learn.

example.title: Anchored scoring matrix
example.body: For illustration, assign strategy 25%, value 30%, feasibility 20%, data readiness 15%, and adoption 10%. Score each criterion from one (weak) to five (strong). Adviser search scores 5, 4, 4, 3, 4: 1.25 + 1.20 + 0.80 + 0.45 + 0.40 = 4.10. Onboarding routing scores 3, 3, 5, 5, 5: 3.90. Fraud alert scores 4, 5, 2, 2, 3: 3.50. Each score requires an evidence note; the values are invented for practice. An eligibility gate separately requires an authorized data use, sponsor, and workable response to consequential errors. A failed gate blocks scale regardless of total.

exercise.title: Define the scales
exercise.body: Create one-to-five anchors for value, feasibility, and risk for your organization. Score two candidate uses, then list the raw evidence behind each rating and a fact that would change it.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: context, measurement, risk response
NIST AI RMF Playbook: Manage tradeoffs

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Compare unlike investments
parts.body:
A service copilot and a fraud alert system should not be compared on a single labor-saving estimate. The copilot may affect many cases with small per-case gains; fraud alerts may protect fewer cases with large potential loss, but false positives can delay legitimate customers. Compare expected benefit, adverse outcomes, control cost, and how quickly evidence can be obtained. Present a range under conservative, central, and favorable assumptions.

Use a simple calculation to expose the tradeoff. Suppose the service copilot could save five minutes on 100,000 eligible cases, with 50% adoption and two minutes of review cost. The net capacity case is 2,500 hours before implementation costs. Suppose fraud alerts might prevent 40 losses worth $10,000 each but trigger 200 extra reviews at $100 and some customer friction. The latter's benefit is highly sensitive to whether the prevented losses are truly incremental. These figures are teaching assumptions, not forecasts.

The decision can differ by horizon. A proven copilot may receive scale funding while a fraud system gets a capped discovery budget to measure precision, false positives, and current loss rates. State any legal classification and affected-person review before testing consequential uses. The EU AI Act lists certain uses in Annex III, including some creditworthiness and insurance risk applications, but classification depends on the system's intended purpose. A fraud detection example should not be labeled high risk solely because it uses AI.

example.title: A split allocation
example.body: Fund the service copilot's controlled pilot and reserve a smaller amount for fraud discovery. The next fraud gate asks for verified baseline losses, alert precision, review capacity, and the cost imposed on legitimate customers.

exercise.title: Build two scenarios
exercise.body: For a high-volume efficiency use and a low-volume risk use, calculate conservative and favorable benefit ranges. Include correction or false-positive costs, write the next evidence gate, and explain what each gets funded now.

sources: EU AI Act Service Desk: Annex III

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Test rankings and balance horizons
parts.body:
After scoring, vary the weights and uncertain inputs. If the top two proposals reverse when risk or adoption weight changes slightly, do not report their ordering as settled. Show a sensitivity table with the conditions under which each wins. Commission a focused test if the uncertainty can be reduced cheaply. If the ranking stays stable across plausible assumptions, the committee can make a stronger allocation decision.

Balance the portfolio by stage, horizon, and shared dependency. A dozen small pilots that all require the same restricted dataset are not diversified. Nor is a mix of impressive demonstrations diversified if no team can adopt them. Reserve capacity for near-term workflow gains, strategic experiments, data or platform foundations, and stopping work that has lost its case. The exact proportions depend on company strategy and available capital. Expose concentration in one provider, process, or group of scarce specialists.

Use a quarterly review to reallocate funds. Compare promised and observed benefit with total cost, quality, adoption, incidents, and dependency progress. Require a sponsor to explain both a request for scale and a request to continue an underperforming pilot. A sensible stop decision releases staff and budget for a stronger opportunity; count that as portfolio discipline. NIST's Manage function describes prioritizing and responding to risk as evidence changes.

example.title: A rank reversal
example.body: Using the matrix in the first part, adviser search leads onboarding routing 4.10 to 3.90. Move ten weight points from strategy to data readiness, producing weights of 15%, 30%, 20%, 25%, and 10%. Search falls to 3.90 and routing rises to 4.10. The committee can fund a small permissions and source-quality test to learn whether search's data score should improve, while a bounded routing pilot proceeds.

exercise.title: Stress-test a ranking
exercise.body: Score three ideas, then change one weight and one uncertain assumption across plausible bounds. Report any rank reversal, the cheapest useful test, and the portfolio decision you would make before its result arrives.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: ongoing monitoring and risk decisions

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Make a funding recommendation
parts.body:
An executive portfolio memo should show the decision it asks for. Name the candidates, current stage, sponsor, investment requested, value range, main uncertainty, unacceptable outcomes, and next gate. Separate committed scale spending from option spending that buys information. The CAIO can recommend the allocation and maintain the evidence standard; the appropriate investment forum and business executives make the capital decisions under the organization's charter.

For a 12-use-case portfolio, identify a small number of lighthouse pilots that can demonstrate a full operating path, scale candidates with measured outcomes, and experiments that answer a strategic uncertainty. Those labels do not guarantee fixed counts or budgets. If the homework asks for three, five, and four, treat them as a planning exercise and challenge whether the evidence supports that distribution. Show dependencies, such as a shared permissions service needed by several ideas, so the committee can fund foundations once and attribute benefits carefully.

A funding recommendation should survive a difficult question: what would you stop next quarter? Give every active item a review date and decision threshold. Include a countermeasure for customer or worker harm and an escalation route for a material incident. The portfolio is a set of reversible bets where possible, with explicit ownership when a decision has lasting effects.

example.title: A recommendation from the matrix
example.body: Give onboarding routing a capped pilot because its readiness and adoption scores are strong across the tested weights. Fund a short permissions and source-quality discovery test for adviser search before its scale decision. Keep fraud alert in discovery until an authorized data use, review capacity, and consequential-error response satisfy the eligibility gate. All scores and allocations are illustrative.

exercise.title: Present the portfolio
exercise.body: Prepare a one-page table for 12 candidates with stage, sponsor, value range, confidence, dependency, requested funding, and next gate. Pick three decisions the investment forum must make and one candidate you recommend stopping.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: Govern and Manage
